idiom_name: impl Drop + ownership on the owner struct (std::mem::drop for early release)
implementation_notes: In Rust, RAII is the default rather than an idiom: a value owns what it holds, the compiler inserts Drop::drop at the end of the owner's lifetime - including early returns and unwinding panics, in reverse order of declaration - and moving the owner transfers the responsibility, so the classic owner class becomes a struct plus impl Drop. The standard library already ships the guards for common resources (File, TcpStream, MutexGuard, Box/Rc/Arc, the CString family), and the escape hatches are explicit: std::mem::drop releases early, ManuallyDrop suppresses the drop, mem::forget leaks by consuming the owner, and Rc/Arc cycles or leaked boxes keep the resource alive forever. Drop::drop cannot fail and cannot be async, so anything whose failure matters (flush, fsync, commit, graceful shutdown) is an explicit method called before the guard dies.
pitfalls: Drop glue does not run on std::process::abort, mem::forget, ManuallyDrop or a hard kill, and drop() cannot return an error: cleanup that must be observed (fsync, commit, a graceful close) has to be an explicit call before the guard leaves scope.
Reference cycles (Rc<RefCell<_>> pairs), leaked boxes and Box::leak'd owners never drop; RAII only guarantees release if the owner itself is dropped, and Rust lets you leak on purpose.

Dropping a guard at the wrong point is a semantic bug the compiler accepts: a MutexGuard held across a borrow or an early return keeps the resource held longer than intended (and across .await it is rejected as non-Send), so bind guards to the narrowest scope.
